newsitem.title: USA: U.S. swap spreads stay mostly steady after FOMC. [CORRECTED 23:15 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. swap spreads stay mostly steady after FOMC. [CORRECTED 23:15 GMT]

text.p: U.S. interest rate swap spreads were mostly steady on Wednesday as the Federal Reserve kept interest rates unchanged at its two-day Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.
"Almost everyone anticipated the Fed wouldn't do anything," said a U.S. bank trader in the West Coast. "Consequently, I wouldn't expect to see any changes (in swap spreads near term)."
Traders said there was some two-way interest in the 10-year spread, trading at around 38-1/2 basis points, where it has been drifting for most of this week.
Traders said there was also some interest in the 30-year maturity, with a deal going through at about 31-5/8 bps. The 30-year was bid at 30-1/2 bps and offered at 32 bps at the close.
At the shorter end of the curve, the two-year spread was roughly unchanged on the day at around 28-1/4 bps bid and 29 bps offered after gradually inching up in the past week or so.
Three-years were somewhat better bid toward the close, pegged at 26-3/4 bps versus 27-1/4 bps.
A swaps broker in New York said the buying was likely to have stemmed from dealer position adjustments.
He added that the market has not seen a trend to speak of in recent weeks and was likely to stay calm for a while.
With a long weekend due to the Independence Day holiday on Friday approaching, traders said activity was slow and many in the market were taking Thursday (corrects day from Friday) off.
Still, some anticipated Friday's June U.S. employment report could determine the market's near-term direction.

A strong reading in the jobs data would likely stimulate views still smouldering in the market that the Fed would have to raise interest rates later in the year, spurring interest to pay fixed rates, they said.
According to a Reuters poll, economists on average expected a rise of 222,000 in non-farm payrolls in June against a gain of 138,000 in May.
The FOMC is due to next meet on August 19.

Late on Thursday (corrects day from Friday), the Fed is due to release the minutes of their May FOMC meeting. It opted to keep interest rates steady at that May meeting, but many market-watchers have suspected the FOMC policy-makers had agreed on a bias towards tightening.
